lead: A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces that do not share a line of action. It has no net force, only a turning effect. The couple moment is M = F d, where F is the force magnitude and d is the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action. This moment is a free vector: it is the same about every point and can be drawn anywhere on the body. Engineers use couples to model steering wheels, taps, screwdrivers and any pure twist. A force moved to a new point becomes a force plus a couple, called a force-couple system.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for moving a force along its line of action, and Chapter 2.2 for the moment of a force about a point and an axis.

blocks.text: Take two forces of equal magnitude F. They are opposite in direction and parallel. Their lines of action are separated by a perpendicular distance d. If the lines are not the same, the two forces form a couple. A couple has zero resultant force, so it cannot move the body as a whole. It only tends to rotate the body. A steering wheel turned by two hands is a common picture: one hand pushes up, the other pulls down, with equal forces. The moment of a couple has magnitude M = F d. The unit is N·m. In two dimensions, choose counterclockwise as positive. Then a clockwise couple is negative. In three dimensions the couple vector is perpendicular to the plane of the two forces. Its sense follows the right-hand rule: curl the fingers in the sense in which the couple tends to rotate the body, and the thumb gives the couple vector. Looking along the vector, the couple turns the body counterclockwise. A couple with d = 0 is not a couple; the forces cancel along one line. Do not call a single force a couple.

blocks.where: F is the magnitude of each force, in N; d is the perpendicular distance between their lines of action, in m; M is the couple moment, in N·m.

sections.h3: The couple moment is a free vector

blocks.text: Choose any point P. The moment of the couple about P is the sum of the moments of the two forces: (r₁ − r_P) × F + (r₂ − r_P) × (−F) = (r₁ − r₂) × F. The term in r_P drops out, so the sum is F d and does not depend on P. This is why a couple moment is called a free vector. You may draw it at any point of the rigid body, and it produces the same external effect. Two couples with the same M are equivalent. They may have different F and d; only the product F d and the sense matter. For example, 40 N at 0.5 m and 100 N at 0.2 m both give 20 N·m. Couples add as vectors. In one plane, add their signed scalar moments. In three dimensions, add their vectors. The moment of a couple about a line is the projection of the couple vector on the unit vector of the line.

blocks.where: M is the couple vector, in N·m; u is the unit vector along the line; M_line is the scalar moment about the line, in N·m.

blocks.text: Suppose a force F acts at point A. You want the same external effect with a force at point O. Add a pair of forces at O: F and −F. They cancel, so nothing changes. Now the original F at A and the −F at O form a couple. The remaining F acts at O. The result is a force F at O plus a couple M = r × F. Here r is the position vector from O to A. In a plane, M = x F_y − y F_x, where x and y are the coordinates of A relative to O. The sign of M follows the right-hand rule. This step is called translating a force to a parallel position. The force and couple together are a force-couple system. The couple is a free vector, so you can draw it anywhere. Use this to reduce a system of forces to one point; see Chapter 2.5. It also prepares equilibrium equations in Chapter 2.7.

blocks.where: M_O is the couple vector in N·m when the force is moved to O; r is the position vector from O to A, in m; F is the force vector, in N.

figure.caption: The force at A is shifted to O: a cancelling pair is added at O, leaving a 120 N force at O and a 72 N·m clockwise couple.

spec.aria: A 120 N force at A, 0.6 m from O, is shifted to O by adding a cancelling pair of 120 N and −120 N at O, leaving the 120 N force at O plus a 72 N·m clockwise couple.

examples.question: A force of 120 N acts vertically downward at A(0.6, 0) m on a plate. Replace it by an equivalent force-couple system at the origin O. Take i along x and j along y, and counterclockwise positive.
steps: 1. Write the position vector of A from O: r = 0.6 i m. The coordinates are x = 0.6 m and y = 0 m.
2. Write the force: F = −120 j N, so F_x = 0 and F_y = −120 N.
3. Compute the moment about O: M_O = r × F = x F_y − y F_x = (0.6)(−120) − (0)(0) = −72 N·m.
4. Read the sign: the vector is −72 k N·m, where k is out of the page. The minus sign means clockwise. The magnitude is 72 N·m.
5. State the equivalent system at O: force F = −120 j N, that is 120 N vertically down, plus a couple M = −72 k N·m, that is 72 N·m clockwise.

6. Check the free-vector property: the couple in this system is a free vector, so its 72 N·m bending effect can be drawn anywhere on the plate. But the couple belongs to the force-couple system. If the force is translated to a different point O', the force stays 120 N downward and the couple changes to r' × F, because the moment arm from O' to A is different.
examples.answer: At O, the equivalent system is a 120 N force vertically downward plus a clockwise couple of 72 N·m (vector −72k N·m).
examples.check:
x = 0.6
y = 0.0
Fx = 0.0
Fy = -120.0
M = x*Fy - y*Fx
print(M)
print(abs(M))

traps: Thinking the couple moment changes when you choose another reference point. It does not; a couple moment is a free vector.
Using the distance between the two points of application instead of the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action.
Adding the two forces of a couple to get a nonzero resultant. The resultant force of a couple is zero.
Writing the unit of a couple moment as N/m or J. The correct unit is N·m.
Confusing a force-couple system with two separate loads. The couple is the moment of the shifted force about the new point.

quiz.a: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action; the net force is zero and the couple moment is Fd.

quiz.q: Why is a couple moment called a free vector?
quiz.a: Its moment about any point is the same Fd, so it can be placed anywhere on the rigid body without changing the external effect.

quiz.q: Two 80 N forces form a couple. The perpendicular distance between their lines of action is 0.25 m. Find the couple moment.
A force F = −50j N acts at A(0.4, 0.3) m. Replace it at O. Find M_O.
quiz.a: x = 0.4 m, y = 0.3 m, F_x = 0, F_y = −50 N. M_O = x F_y − y F_x = (0.4)(−50) − (0)(0) = −20 N·m, that is 20 N·m clockwise.

quiz.q: A couple is moved from the middle of a plate to a corner. Does the external effect change? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A couple moment is a free vector; its moment is the same about every point of the rigid body.

quiz.q: A force at A is translated to O. If O is moved 1 m to the right, does the force vector at the new point change? Does the couple change?
quiz.a: The force vector is unchanged. The couple changes because r changes: M = r × F, so the moment arm changes.

quiz.q: Write the formula for the moment of a couple about a line.
quiz.a: M_line = M · u, where M is the couple vector and u is the unit vector along the line.

beyond: Not for the exam. In robotics, any force-couple system can be reduced, at a suitable point, to a single force plus a couple parallel to it; this six-number package is called a wrench, and it is used to describe contact and motion. In finite element software, the same idea lets a load applied away from a node be moved to that node with an added moment. Screw theory builds on free couple vectors to describe twists and wrenches. Search next for “force-couple system wrench” and “screw theory statics”.
